claim: Peter Bright, a former technology editor at the publication Ars Technica who used the social-media handle @DrPizza, was convicted at trial in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York in March 2020 of one count of attempted enticement of a minor to engage in illegal sexual activity — a charge carrying a mandatory minimum of ten years and a maximum of life. Federal prosecutors showed that in April 2019 Bright contacted an undercover FBI agent posing as the mother of a seven-year-old girl and a nine-year-old boy and, over hundreds of messages, discussed meeting the children for sexual activity; he was arrested in May 2019 after traveling to a New York City park to meet the agent and beginning to walk toward the purported children's residence. On November 4, 2020 the court sentenced him to 144 months (12 years) in federal prison.

sources.label: U.S. Attorney's Office, S.D.N.Y. — "Former Journalist Convicted At Trial Of Attempted Child Enticement" (DOJ press release on the March 2020 conviction).

notes: Group-A record: the conviction is a documented court fact. The reel's hook — that Bright, under @DrPizza, repeatedly mocked Pizzagate as 'nonsense'/'baseless' and called believers 'morons' before his own arrest — is NOT supported by the archived record and is not adopted. A Wayback Machine review of @DrPizza's tweets found the only documented Pizzagate tweet to be a self-deprecating joke ('As someone named DrPizza I dread to think what my involvement in pizzagate will turn out to be,' May 9, 2017), not the dismissive mockery the reel describes; the broader characterization could not be verified. The verified fact here is narrowly the SDNY conviction. Bright faced a 10-year mandatory minimum and was sentenced to 144 months on November 4, 2020 (sentence length confirmed via Inner City Press SDNY trial coverage). He does not appear in the EFTA Epstein corpus in any relevant way.
